title: 3-Read Friday #74: Retrieval Strength, the Area Model, and I/We/You
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #74 gathers three posts unified by a shared concern for pedagogical models that are powerful in principle but easily flattened into rigid procedure. Dylan Kane offers what Barton calls the best visualisation he has seen of the distinction between retrieval strength (how easily a memory can be recalled right now) and storage strength (how durable that memory is long-term), showing that spaced, effortful retrieval builds storage strength far more than repeated easy exposure. Jon Fant provides a detailed walkthrough of the area model as a single representational thread that can carry students from early array-based multiplication all the way to polynomial division and factorisation, echoing Barton's own view that maths teachers should choose methods that scale with conceptual complexity rather than discarding and replacing them. Rachel Ball and Alex Fairlamb caution against turning the I/We/You gradual-release framework into a rigid, timed lesson structure enforced for compliance purposes, arguing it works best as a flexible continuum responsive to real-time checks for understanding. Barton's editorial thread across all three: good pedagogical models earn their power from flexible, principled use, not from being mechanically applied.
points: Dylan Kane's retrieval-strength/storage-strength model, which Barton calls the best visualisation of the concept he has seen, shows that storage strength (long-term durability) increases most when retrieval happens with effort - after some forgetting - rather than through easy, repeated exposure.

Jon Fant's area-model deep dive traces a single coherent representation from early array-based multiplication (ages 4-5) through multi-digit multiplication, factorisation, completing the square, and polynomial division - illustrating Barton's own principle that maths methods should be chosen for their capacity to scale with complexity.

Rachel Ball and Alex Fairlamb's central warning: I/We/You is a powerful way to conceptualise a learning cycle but becomes 'painfully flawed' when schools enforce it as a rigid, timed lesson structure that ignores real-time checks for understanding.

Ball and Fairlamb report that teachers have been told to be 'on' the independent-practice phase by a fixed time, checked by observers - evidence that a flexible pedagogical model has, in some schools, mutated into a compliance-driven mandate.

A shared thread Barton draws out across all three posts: pedagogical frameworks (retrieval, the area model, I/We/You) are valuable specifically because they are principled and adaptable - rigidly proceduralising any of them undermines the thinking they are meant to support.
quotes: Big claim alert, but this is the best visualisation of the distinction between the retrieval and storage strengths of memories -- and why this matters -- that I have ever seen. It could be shared with students and colleagues alike.
Recently, I argued that maths teachers should choose methods that can be built upon as concepts become more complex.
Here, Jon provides a wonderful deep dive into how one particular method -- the area model -- can take students from multiplication to polynomial division.

A detailed post, using examples from several different subjects, that argues that whilst I/We/You is a powerful way to plan and execute a learning cycle, as a rigid lesson structure, it is painfully flawed
